title: What Happens When Clashing Ink Slows Every Reader Down?
description:
Clinical Case Briefing — J. Ridley Stroop (1935): Why You Cannot Stop Reading the Word 'RED' Printed in Blue Ink, grounded in J. R. Stroop (1935) (Journal of Experimental Psychology). Empirical findings show that in 1935 at George Peabody College in Nashville, doctoral student J. Ridley Stroop tested college undergraduates across 3 elegant cardstock-and-stopwatch experiments using 10×10 grids of 100 items printed in red, blue, green, brown, and purple.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how primary visual cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that experiment 1 carried the first shock: reading color WORDS aloud when printed in mismatched ink ('RED' in blue ink) took 43.3 seconds vs 41.0 seconds in black ink — virtually ZERO interference (+2.3 s, just 5.6%).

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- J. R. Stroop (1935). Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions. Journal of Experimental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0054651
- Colin M. MacLeod (1991). John Ridley Stroop: Creator of a landmark cognitive task. Canadian Psychology / Psychologie canadienne. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0079012
- Sirawaj Itthipuripat, Sean Deering, John T Serences (2019). When Conflict Cannot be Avoided: Relative Contributions of Early Selection and Frontal Executive Control in Mitigating Stroop Conflict. Cerebral Cortex. https://doi.org/10.1093/cercor/bhz042
